title: West Woods
summary: West Woods is a forty acre beach and woodland area owned by the Shinnecock Tribe. The woodland and beach area is used for contemporary social gatherings, weddings, celebrations, camping, and sweat lodge ceremonies. In recent times, West Woods has been encroached upon with it's blurred boundaries. At the start of the 1747 100-year timber lease to the Shinnecock by Southampton Town, the land encompassed one hundred acres.
activity_update_summary: Added a section on contemporary sweat lodge and coming-of-age ceremonies, with the sweat lodge photograph and associated plant observations and community contributions.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: This forty-acre tract of beach and woodland serves as an active, contemporary gathering space where Shinnecock tribal members continue to host community weddings and sweat lodge ceremonies. Defending these vital communal spaces against modern boundary encroachment demonstrates that Native cultural practices are living traditions permanently rooted in the Long Island landscape.
history_content:
1885 During a Shinnecock Tribal Meeting, the tribe voted that the tribe defend any one who might be sued for cutting wood in the west woods. 1 The earliest record of West Woods appears in Belcher Hyde's 1916 map. Again in the later 1929 Dolph Stewart map.

Westwoods public land-rights source

A Dans Papers article on Westwoods described the area through a public land-rights dispute rather than as empty shoreline. It supports the Cassady-related calendar entry by showing Westwoods as part of a continuing Shinnecock sovereignty and land-defense history.

Source: Dans Papers, Sorting Out a 350 Year Old Real Estate Sale, project archive / Shinnecock Archaeology and History Drive folder.

Sweat Lodge and Coming-of-Age Ceremonies

West Woods remains a place of contemporary Shinnecock ceremonial life. Tribal members gather here for seasonal sweat lodge ceremonies and for initiation ceremonies marking young people’s coming of age.

Resources remembered by Shinnecock elders

The Shinnecock Environmental Department’s 2014 catalogue names West Woods in its resource accounts. These sections preserve the places named in that 2014 community record. Present-day access, abundance, and harvesting rules may differ.

Eastern white pine and pine materials

Pine pitch served as a sealant for containers and structures, and pine supplied building material. The catalogue also records food and medicinal traditions, placing trees within the work of making and maintaining a home. PDF p. 16.

Cranberries in Shinnecock memory

Elders remembered cranberries around Heady Creek and Church Street before the 1938 hurricane. The catalogue connects berries with food preservation and dyes used on woven materials. It also records concerns about changes to berry-growing places. PDF p. 18.

Huckleberries

Huckleberries appear as an important part of Shinnecock food life, gathered with other berries and used in pies. The catalogue names dwarf and blue huckleberries and connects berry knowledge with woodland edges. PDF p. 18.

Highbush and lowbush blueberries

Elders recalled berry picking on Shinnecock lands, at West Woods, and in the Pine Barrens. The catalogue describes berries dried for later use, used with meat, and added to samp with corn. Gathering and preservation extended the value of a short season. PDF pp. 19–20.

Spicebush

The catalogue names spicebush in the West Woods and museum vicinity, within an account of aromatic plants used in Shinnecock households. PDF p. 21.

Explore all resources and places in the catalogue.

Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders, April 4, 2014, PDF pp. 16, 18, 19, 20, 21. Page numbers count the cover as PDF page 1.

Continuing land defense at Westwoods

On January 2, 2025, the Shinnecock Nation Council of Trustees announced that the U.S. Department of the Interior had reaffirmed Westwoods as restricted fee land held by the Nation. The Council reported that its metes and bounds had been entered in the Bureau of Indian Affairs land-record system. This was an acknowledgment of the land status the Nation maintained, not an announcement that Shinnecock history there had just begun.

Westwoods remains a place of Shinnecock community life and land defense. It is private tribal land, not a public recreation destination. The shaded area on this map is an approximate historical orientation and does not reproduce the federal land record or establish a legal boundary.

Shinnecock Nation Council of Trustees, Land Determination, January 2, 2025, updated January 7, 2025.
